0.title: Knowing That You Are His
0.essay:
Is it possible to know — really know, with settled confidence — that you belong to God? Or is the Christian life bound to be marked by constant uncertainty, with assurance kept for the exceptionally holy or the dangerously presumptuous?

The deepest fear

This question has troubled sincere believers for centuries. The person who prays, “Lord, I want to be saved — but am I really?” is not asking an abstract question. They are asking whether the deepest fear of the human heart, that I am not truly known and loved by God, is true or false. And Scripture’s answer is glorious: “I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). Know. Not hope dimly, not suspect tentatively, but know.

Possible, normal and given

The Reformed tradition has always held that assurance — settled confidence of one’s salvation — is possible, normal and the birthright of every true believer. That does not mean it is always fully felt; few things in the Christian life are. It means that God has given the means by which his children may know they are his: the promises of the gospel, the witness of the Spirit, and the evidence of grace in a life.

Looking in the right place

Many believers struggle with assurance not because they lack grounds for it but because they look in the wrong place. Whoever searches their feelings for certainty will always be disappointed. Whoever looks to Christ — his perfect obedience, his finished atonement, his resurrection power, his unbreakable promises — will find more assurance than their heart can hold.

The chapters

The Ground of Assurance: The Finished Work of Christ; The Promises of God — anchors for the doubting soul; The Spirit’s Witness; Perseverance — those who are his will not be lost; Assurance and Self-Examination; and Living from Assurance. For further reading: the Westminster Confession, chapter 18; Calvin’s Institutes 3.2; Thomas Brooks, Heaven on Earth; and Sinclair Ferguson, Children of the Living God.

1.title: The Ground of Assurance: The Finished Work of Christ
1.essay:
The first ground of assurance is not your spiritual experience, your moral progress or your consistency in prayer. It is the finished work of Jesus Christ.

It is finished

On the cross Jesus said, “It is finished” (John 19:30). In Greek it is one word, tetelestai, and its tense describes a completed action with lasting effect: it has been finished and stays finished. The debt of our sin, the sentence of the law, the demand of God’s justice — all of it was paid in full. There is no outstanding balance and nothing left for the believer to add. The bedrock of assurance is not “I have done enough” but “he has done it all”.

This was the Reformation’s great recovery after centuries of uncertainty. Justification is not a process by which we become more and more righteous; it is a verdict by which we are declared righteous on the basis of Christ’s righteousness credited to us. “For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21). Our sin to him, his righteousness to us: complete, final and irreversible. Our standing before God is as secure as Christ’s, because it is his standing we share. When doubt whispers, “You are not righteous enough,” the gospel answers, “You have been given the righteousness of God in Christ.”

No condemnation

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Not reduced condemnation, not suspended or conditional condemnation — none. The case is closed. And the verdict cannot be overturned on appeal, because the one who gave it is also the one against whom the crime was committed, and he has been satisfied. Someone who lives under that verdict can face their sin honestly, their death peacefully and each new day with confidence.

Perfected, and being sanctified

“For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Notice the two tenses. “Has perfected” is finished; “are being sanctified” is still going on. Our holiness is partial; our standing is complete. The ongoing work of becoming holy does not endanger the finished fact of being accepted. That is why assurance and an ongoing struggle with sin are not contradictions.

As stable as Christ

If assurance rests on the finished work of Christ rather than on the ongoing work in us, it can be as stable as Christ himself. He does not waver. His obedience is perfect and permanent, his atonement complete, and his resurrection shows that the Father accepted his sacrifice. The believer who grasps this stands on rock, not sand. Doubt, dryness, failure and discouragement cannot wash the foundation away, because the foundation is not our experience but his accomplishment.

Outside us

The Westminster Confession teaches that assurance rests on “the divine truth of the promises of salvation, the inward evidence of those graces unto which these promises are made, the testimony of the Spirit of adoption witnessing with our spirits that we are the children of God”. But the first ground is always the promises — the objective word of the gospel, outside us. Calvin defined faith as a firm and certain knowledge of God’s goodwill toward us, grounded on his promise in Christ. Assurance is not a mystical experience floating free of the promises; it is confident trust in them.

Look to the wounds

In the depths of his spiritual anguish, Martin Luther was told by his confessor, Staupitz, not to examine his sins more carefully but to look to the wounds of Christ. That was the Reformation in miniature: a turn from inward examination to outward faith.

A woman in a prayer group confesses that she has been a Christian for twenty years but has never been sure she is truly saved. Her pastor asks, “Do you believe Christ died for sinners?” She says yes. “Are you a sinner?” Yes. “Then he died for you.” The outward promise, plainly applied, does what no amount of inward searching could.

For reflection

Where do you usually look first when you doubt your salvation? What difference does “It is finished” make to that? How does Hebrews 10:14 help you hold together assurance and your ongoing struggle with sin? How would you answer the pastor’s three questions?

2.title: The Promises of God: Anchors for the Doubting Soul
2.essay:
God is not coy about the salvation of his people. Scripture is full of promises — plain, repeated and meant to give confidence to those who receive them.

Not probabilities

“Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life” (John 3:36). “For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). These are not probability statements. They are covenant promises from the God who “is not man, that he should lie” (Numbers 23:19). And they outlast everything: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

The trap of looking at yourself

The problem is not that the promises are unclear, but that we find it hard to believe they apply to us. We read “whoever believes” and immediately ask, “But do I really believe?” We read “my sheep hear my voice” and wonder whether we are really his sheep. That is natural, but it becomes a trap when it makes us look away from the promise and toward ourselves. The promise is not “whoever believes with sufficient clarity”; it is “whoever believes”. The object of faith, Christ, matters far more than the quality of our faith, which will always be imperfect.

Look at Romans 10:13 again: “everyone”. Not the worthy, the holy or the certain. Calling on the Lord is an act of need, not achievement — the cry of a beggar, not the presentation of a performer. If you have called on Christ, even trembling and full of doubts, the promise holds.

In his hands

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand. My Father, who has given them to me, is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father’s hand” (John 10:27–29). Three layers of security: in the hand of Christ, given by the Father, held by the Father who is greater than all. No one — not Satan, not the world, not our own weakness — can snatch the sheep away. “They will never perish.” In the darkest moment, this is the promise to hold: “I am in his hands, not my own.”

Never cast out

“All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). The Father’s purpose and the Son’s promise make an unbreakable chain. In Greek “never” is a double negative, as emphatic as the language allows. Not under any circumstances: not if you fail, not if you doubt, not if you fall. If you have come to him, you will not be cast out. He “is able to save to the uttermost those who draw near to God through him” (Hebrews 7:25).

An anchor

Hebrews gives the doubting soul an image. God “guaranteed it with an oath, so that by two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us. We have this as a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul, a hope that enters into the inner place behind the curtain” (Hebrews 6:17–19). Not a warm feeling that changes with the weather of the soul, but an anchor fixed in God’s presence, holding in every storm. Hope in the New Testament is not wishful thinking; it is confident expectation based on the character of God.

The Westminster Confession calls the promises “divine truth” — not human encouragement or pastoral opinion, but the sworn word of the covenant God. They are particular, given to his people, and universal in offer, given to all who come to Christ. That combination is the engine of assurance.

Word by word

A pastor once sat with a woman in deep distress, convinced she was not saved because she still struggled with sin. He walked her through John 3:16 phrase by phrase. “For God so loved the world” — he loved sinners. “That he gave his only Son” — he gave what was most costly. “That whoever believes in him should not perish” — whoever, including you. “But have eternal life” — not temporary, not contingent, but eternal. By the end she was weeping. The promise had landed.

That is the practice of promise-anchored assurance: take a promise, rest on it and plead it before God. The goal is not to manufacture a feeling of certainty but to train the mind and heart to rest on God’s word. When feelings fail, as they will, the promises remain.

For reflection

Which promise of God do you most need to anchor yourself to right now? Why is the object of faith more important than the strength of your faith? Choose one promise from this chapter, learn it by heart this week, and pray it back to God when doubt comes.

3.title: The Spirit’s Witness: Internal Evidence of Grace
3.essay:
The Holy Spirit plays a unique part in a believer’s assurance. He is “the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15) — a personal, inward witness that we are children of God.

Abba

The Spirit of adoption is the opposite of the spirit of slavery. Slavery produces fear; adoption produces closeness. “Abba” is the Aramaic word for father, used by children at home. Jesus used it in Gethsemane, in the deepest moment of his anguish (Mark 14:36), and the Spirit gives us the same closeness, even in anguish. “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16). It is a joint testimony: the Spirit’s voice alongside our own, saying together that we belong.

This witness is not the same as the outward promise, though it never contradicts it, and it is not the same as self-examination, though self-examination may confirm it. Calvin was careful to say that the Spirit’s testimony does not float free of Scripture; it is the Spirit bearing witness through and with the word to the heart.

Usually quiet

The Spirit’s witness is often misunderstood. Some treat it as a mystical flood of certainty that descends without warning. God can give such experiences, and has to many saints. But his usual testimony is quieter: the peace that “surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7), the sense that God is Father and not only Judge, the inclination to pray, love for God’s people, the conviction that Jesus is Lord. These are not flashy, but they are real, and when we notice them they are deeply reassuring.

John Wesley described an evening in Aldersgate Street, London, on 24 May 1738: “I felt my heart strangely warmed. I felt I did trust in Christ, Christ alone for salvation, and an assurance was given me that he had taken away my sins, even mine.” That was the Spirit’s witness in dramatic form. Most believers know something quieter. A grandmother who has prayed for decades simply knows, with a calm certainty no argument could shake, that she is God’s. She cannot point to one dramatic moment. She points to a lifetime of the Spirit’s quiet presence: love for God’s word, prayers addressed to a real Person, and the people of God she has loved and been loved by. Both are real.

The fruit he grows

The Spirit also produces fruit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). These are evidence of his presence, and so of real new birth. Someone who loves God’s people, knows a joy that does not depend on circumstances, has a peace that steadies them in crisis, and shows patience they could never produce alone, is showing signs of the Spirit. No one displays all of them perfectly. But their presence in any degree is evidence of grace. Looking for fruit is meant to encourage — “See, the Spirit is here” — not to torment — “You don’t have enough.”

Love for the brothers

John offers a striking test: “We know that we have passed out of death into life, because we love the brothers” (1 John 3:14). Not only warm feelings, but the practical, self-giving love that mirrors Christ’s. That love cannot be manufactured by good intentions or social obligation. Where it exists, even imperfectly, it is a sign of the Spirit’s work. And it is never a reason for self-congratulation, only for gratitude: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). John’s whole first letter is almost a manual for this kind of Spirit-enabled self-examination: “By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and obey his commandments” (1 John 5:2).

The seal and the down payment

Believers “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance” (Ephesians 1:13–14). The word for guarantee means a deposit, the first instalment of what will be ours in full in the new creation. The seal is God’s own mark of ownership: “This one is mine.” It cannot be broken by our weakness or wavering, because it is God’s act, not ours. The indwelling Spirit is himself the assurance.

A double cord

The Westminster Confession lists “the inward evidence of those graces” and “the testimony of the Spirit of adoption” as two of the three grounds of assurance, alongside the promises. They are distinct but related. The fruit is evidence; the Spirit’s witness is testimony. The testimony is more immediate; the evidence more sustained. Together they make a double cord.

For reflection

Do you find it natural to call God “Father”? What might that tell you? Which of the quiet signs of the Spirit can you see in your own life? Who are “the brothers” you love, and how does that love show itself? Thank God for one specific fruit of the Spirit he has grown in you.

4.title: Perseverance: Those Who Are His Will Not Be Lost
4.essay:
The perseverance of the saints — the fifth point of the doctrines of grace — is among the most comforting truths in Scripture. Those who have been truly born again and justified will persevere in faith to the end, not because of their own strength, but because God “who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

The weight on God

Paul’s confidence is not in the Philippians but in God, who began and will complete. The work has a divine author and a divine completion date. Between the beginning and the end there may be struggles, failures and long seasons of weakness. But the one who started cannot fail to finish. The verse does not say, “If you persevere, you will be saved,” which puts the weight on you. It says, “He who began will complete,” which puts the weight on God, where it belongs. Perseverance is not a human achievement but divine preservation.

The Father’s will

“And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39). The security of believers is not incidental to God’s plan; it is the will of God. Jesus has been given his people by the Father, and he will raise every one at the last day. Father and Son are committed to keeping every one of God’s people, and the Spirit is the seal until that day.

Those who went out

Scripture also speaks of people who seem to be believers and then fall away finally (Hebrews 6:4–6). John explains: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have continued with us” (1 John 2:19). Final departure shows that someone never truly belonged; it does not mean a true believer lost their salvation. That is not cold logic but pastoral protection. If you were truly born again, you will not fall away finally. And the very fact that you fear falling away is itself evidence that the Spirit is present. People who do not know God rarely lose sleep over leaving him.

True believers can fall grievously and for seasons, as David and Peter did. The Canons of Dort say plainly that the saints may fall into great and serious sins, with real loss of assurance, deep grief and serious consequences. But God never lets them lose the grace of adoption or the state of justification; by his Spirit he renews them to true repentance. The Westminster Confession says that those God has accepted and called “can neither totally nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved”. That “shall certainly” is the voice of the covenant God.

Nothing

“For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38–39). Paul names every threat he can think of and dismisses it, reaching for the farthest edges of existence. The love of God is not a feeling that comes and goes. It is a bond secured in the covenant, purchased by Christ’s blood, sealed by the Spirit and guarded by God’s power. Nothing can break it.

Not a licence

None of this licenses carelessness. As a slogan, “once saved, always saved” can produce a lazy, presumptuous faith. The Reformed tradition always holds perseverance together with the means by which God keeps his people: word, sacrament, prayer, fellowship and discipline. True Christians use these not to earn salvation but as the expression of the faith the Spirit has given. Perseverance is certain — and the person who is sure of it will be persevering.

Peter’s fall

On the night of Jesus’ arrest, Peter denied him three times, publicly and with an oath: “Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, ‘I do not know the man’” (Matthew 26:74). If anyone seemed to have thrown away his salvation, it was Peter. But Jesus had told him beforehand, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail. And when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:32). Jesus knew the fall was coming, prayed him through it, and expected his restoration. The threefold “Do you love me?” on the beach (John 21:15–17) is one of the most beautiful scenes in Scripture. The God who keeps his people keeps them even through their falls. The fall is not the end of the story.

For reflection

Why is it better news that God will complete his work than that you must persevere? How does 1 John 2:19 comfort the fearful without excusing the careless? Which of the means of grace do you most need to use more faithfully? What does Jesus’ prayer for Peter tell you about his prayers for you?

5.title: Assurance and Self-Examination: How to Look Inward Rightly
5.essay:
The Reformed tradition has always affirmed both full assurance and the importance of self-examination. They do not contradict each other, but they are easily confused in practice. Everything depends on the order.

Examine yourselves

Self-examination is biblical: “Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?” (2 Corinthians 13:5). Notice the assumption behind Paul’s question. He expects them to find evidence of Christ’s presence. Self-examination in the New Testament is not a test designed to produce failure but a search designed to find grace. Someone who finds no evidence at all may indeed be unbelieving; that was Paul’s worry about some in Corinth. But someone who finds imperfect, partial, weak evidence of the Spirit’s work has found enough. Weak faith is still faith.

The right order

Self-examination becomes dangerous when it is the first ground of assurance instead of a secondary confirmation. Whoever looks inward first, and only turns to Christ after passing their own inspection, will be anxious for ever, because “the heart is deceitful above all things” (Jeremiah 17:9) and will never give a clean bill of health.

So look first to Christ — his finished work, his promises, the objective gospel — and then examine yourself for confirming evidence. Self-examination with Christ at the centre asks, “Is there evidence that the Spirit is at work in me?” That is healthy. Self-examination with self at the centre asks, “Am I good enough? Do I feel strongly enough? Have I done enough?” That is a trap.

That you may know

John states the purpose of his first letter: “that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). That is the apostle’s aim: not uncertainty, but knowledge. And the knowledge rests on believing “in the name of the Son of God”, not on a perfect record or an unbroken experience. The tests John gives throughout the letter — love for others, obedience, confession of sin, the Spirit’s witness — are not hurdles to clear before assurance is granted. They are markers that help believers recognise that they do believe. The goal of self-examination is not a passing grade; it is discovering what God has already done.

When you find sin

Honest self-examination will always uncover sin. The response is not despair but confession. “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8–9). Faithful, because he has promised. Just, because the penalty has been paid at the cross, so forgiveness is not a compromise of justice but an expression of it. And confession itself is evidence of grace; unbelievers do not usually come to God in genuine repentance. Self-examination should lead not to condemnation but to the cross.

Bruised reeds

Matthew applies Isaiah’s words about the Servant of the Lord to Jesus: “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (Matthew 12:20). A bruised reed is nearly broken, too damaged to play a note; a smouldering wick is more smoke than flame. That is Jesus’ pastoral policy toward weak faith. He does not stamp out the feeble believer; he tends them. Whoever keeps crawling back to Christ despite failing again and again is under the care of the one who specialises in bruised reeds.

The Puritans were masters of self-examination, and they are sometimes blamed for producing anxiety rather than assurance. There is some justice in that: endless self-scrutiny can become a sickness of its own. But the best of them made self-examination serve assurance. Richard Sibbes wrote a whole book, The Bruised Reed, on this verse. The smallest true evidence of grace is real evidence; the weakest faith is real faith. Someone who can only say, “I want to want God,” is further along than they know. Thomas Brooks listed marks of grace to encourage the weak, not to crush them.

A better question

A man struggles for years with assurance because he knows the depths of his own sin. Every time he examines himself, he finds more to condemn. His pastor suggests a different question. Instead of asking, “How sinful am I?” — which will always produce distress — ask, “Do I hate my sin?” Hatred of sin is itself the Spirit’s work. The man realises that he does hate it. He longs to be free of it, and he keeps coming back to Christ in repentance. That is not the pattern of an unbeliever. It is the pattern of a real Christian who has not yet learned to read the evidence rightly.

For reflection

When you examine yourself, do you start with Christ or with yourself? What changes if you reverse the order? Read 1 John 1:5–2:2. What should you do with the sin self-examination reveals? Do you hate your sin? What does that tell you? Where do you feel like a bruised reed, and how does Jesus treat you there?

6.title: Living from Assurance: Freedom, Obedience, and Joy
6.essay:
Assurance is not the end of the journey; it is the beginning. The believer who is settled in their salvation does not relax into carelessness. They are finally free to obey God from love rather than fear, to serve others from abundance rather than anxiety, to face suffering with hope, and to die without terror.

Assurance fuels holiness

The Reformed tradition has always insisted that assurance and holiness go together; indeed, that assurance drives holiness. Uncertain believers are often paralysed: too afraid to look honestly at their sin in case it confirms their worst fears, too anxious about their own salvation to give themselves to others, too busy asking “Am I saved?” to get on with living as though they are. Assurance breaks the paralysis. Someone who knows they are God’s is free to spend themselves for his glory and their neighbour’s good.

John Piper puts it this way: “God is most glorified in us when we are most satisfied in him.” The believer who is sure of God’s love is the one most able to be satisfied in him, because they are not working to earn his favour but resting in favour already given.

Peace, access and hope

“Therefore, since we have been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we rejoice in hope of the glory of God” (Romans 5:1–2). Peace with God is not first a feeling but a status: the war is over. Access means we stand in grace, permanently, by faith. And hope means our future is secure. Someone who has grasped their justification does not merely know facts; they live differently. They are at peace, they are welcome, they are hopeful.

Confidence for the day of judgment

“By this is love perfected with us, so that we may have confidence for the day of judgment … There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:17–18). The word for confidence means boldness. It is not fearlessness through moral achievement but fearlessness through love received. Believers face the day of judgment with confidence, not because they are faultless, but because their Judge is also their Father.

Diligent, not passive

Peter commands believers to pursue assurance actively: “Therefore, brothers, be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall. For in this way there will be richly provided for you an entrance into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Peter 1:10–11). The qualities are the ones he has just listed: faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, brotherly affection and love (2 Peter 1:5–7). And the promise is not a narrow escape but a rich welcome.

The Westminster Confession says that assurance is not of the essence of faith: someone may have real saving faith while struggling with assurance. But assurance is the fullness faith tends toward, and “it is the duty of every one to give all diligence to make his calling and election sure”. Seeking it is not presumptuous; it is commanded. And the Confession describes its fruit: the heart “enlarged in peace and joy in the Holy Ghost, in love and thankfulness to God, and in strength and cheerfulness in the duties of obedience”.

A weaned child

“But I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother; like a weaned child is my soul within me” (Psalm 131:2). Not the anxious infant crying for milk, but the contented child resting in its mother’s arms, wanting nothing but her presence. The weaned child is not hungry and does not need to cry; it simply rests. That is where assurance leads: not to the excitement of new spiritual experiences or the anxiety of spiritual performance, but to the deep, settled peace of a child held by a love that will never let go.

It is well

Horatio Spafford lost four daughters in a shipwreck in 1873 and later wrote “It Is Well with My Soul”; the story is told that the words came to him as his ship passed near the place where they had drowned. “Whatever my lot, thou hast taught me to say, It is well, it is well with my soul.” That is not the denial of grief — Spafford was devastated — and it is not stoic indifference. It is assurance: “My sin — O the bliss of this glorious thought! — my sin, not in part but the whole, is nailed to the cross, and I bear it no more.” Assurance does not remove suffering. It changes its meaning and its ending.

For reflection

How has uncertainty about your salvation held you back from serving God freely? Which of the three gifts in Romans 5:1–2 do you most need to live in this week? What qualities from 2 Peter 1:5–7 could you pursue more diligently? Read Psalm 131 slowly, and ask God to quiet your soul like a weaned child.
